data.name: Daikatana
data.detailed_description:
In 2455 AD, Kage Mishima used the magical powers of Daikatana, the most powerful sword ever forged, to alter time and establish himself as supreme dictator. You are Hiro Miyamoto, one of the few people on earth who knows what happened. You and your two friends Superfly Johnson & Mikiko Ebihara must travel through time to find the corrupted dictatorship and right the wrongs inflicted on the world.

Key Features:

  • Two highly-trained sidekicks to watch your back
  • More than 50 superior enemies to slice and dice
  • 25 glorious weapons to collect and utilize
  • 24 huge levels that span four time periods
  • Killer multiplayer capabilities for free network play

reviews.review:
The best way I can describe Daikatana is that it's an acquired taste. A lot of people will bounce off of this game for many reasons that I can honestly understand - for instance, the game is full of bullcrap enemy encounters, weapons that can easily self-damage you, a difficult opening episode, hard to see switches necessary for progression and two sidekicks that are more trouble than help. 

I think it's best to contextualize this game before attempting a playthrough. The #1 design goal with Daikatana was to create an "expert level FPS" that was even difficult for John Romero himself to play. This does not mean it's a well-balanced game about mastering its mechanics. Instead, Daikatana is about surviving through cheap encounters that force you to play slow & cautiously despite the insanely fast movement and air control the player has. John Romero's About to Make You His Bitch - it's like he is daring you to take on the challenge of beating this tough game, and I think the first episode fulfills this fantasy.

Here's a few examples of how this concept is executed:
1. The first few levels are in a swamp. The majority of the enemies aren't huge guys with big hitboxes. Instead, you are mainly fighting flying mosquitoes and small frogs that can blend in with the environment. They can be difficult to aim at and playing recklessly can easily put you in a position where you are overwhelmed by them.
2. Your first weapons inflict self-damage if you don't follow their strict rules. The first gun, the Ion Blaster will hurt you if fired underwater. There are definitely a few sections where I had to be mindful of this. The C4 Launcher has huge splash damage that resulted in fragging myself quite a few times. Additionally, the power weapon of the episode shoots a giant wrecking ball that fucks EVERYTHING up including you - it's best to fire and duck for cover with it. Suck it down.
3. Hitscanner enemies that don't give a fuck. This is where I found out that Daikatana prefers a cautious playstyle. Set traps with the C4 Launcher, use the Ion Blaster's ricochet effect to shoot down hallways without exposing yourself... and you feel like a badass.
4. Bullcrap tricks and traps, including unintentional ones, like a couple level loads where enemies are waiting to spawnkill you.
5. A section in the first episode where you are encouraged to use the shotgun, which as a knockback effect on the player, as an airbrake to minimize fall damage. I haven't seen a singleplayer FPS properly use this concept and I was so hyped to see that. That felt 'expert level.'

It's up to you to determine if these examples are indicative of a poorly designed game OR a fun challenge to take on, even if it can have its frustration points. I ended up leaning towards the latter AFTER turning on infinite saves and quicksaving consistently. The original version of the game had limited saves which does not fit the type of game this is.

However, I was disappointed when I realized the second, third and fourth episode are much easier in comparison due to its levelling system. After some playtime, you can raise your characters attributes, like damage, fire rate and health. Playing on hard gives you enough XP to almost fully maximize your stats. It didn't become a cakewalk - but it no longer felt like I had to think about encounters as much, and the "expert level game" design pillar was forgotten as time went on.

The next design goal of Daikatana was to push the amount of content the game had compared to its predecessors. I can confidently say this idea was fully realized and is the best aspect of the game. There are FOUR time periods depicted in this game, with six unique weapons, at least 10 unique enemies, and unique texturework. Your playthrough spans a futuristic facility in a swamp, ancient Greek mythology, a plague-ridden village during the Viking era and 2030 San Francisco where you shoot up Alcatraz prisoners with a sci-fi glock. The environment art can be beautiful and the texture work is fantastic the whole time. Daikatana, above all else, has variety. There are also plenty of unconventional weapons that showed a lot of creativity, like the Nharre's Nightmare staff that draws a pentagram on your screen and summons a demon that kills enemies for you, or the Hammer of Hades that throws you into the air when you slam it on the ground. The Daikatana itself is also a standout weapon when fully levelled that can chew through anything.

The last design goal of Daikatana was to introduce a narrative that strings together all the locations and gives the player two sidekicks to manage throughout the game. Romero did not want them to be helpless pushovers. He wanted them to be like an RPG party, where they are integral to the story and can do everything the player can. The sidekicks can engage in combat, traverse platforming puzzles and collect pickups. I think he was ahead of his time with this concept, but the execution of it is terrible. They constantly get in the way, don't collect pickups when they need them, get stuck in the level and you have to babysit them through the experience. I don't believe the level design was thoughtfully designed for the use of the sidekicks, there are so many vents you crawl through and tight corridors that they have no space to do anything except sit behind you like a bitch and cry about you running into them. No matter how much I love Superfly Johnson's name and attitude, he can get on my nerves during gameplay. There is an option to turn off the sidekicks when playing - I chose not to play this way, but it might be for the best to do so.

I found the story to be interesting but once again the execution of the way its told is terrible. The cutscenes are so long and drawn out and they fuck up the pace of the game. Not much happens visually during them either, the characters bob their heads like puppets as they babble on and on. I wish the story was told more throughout gameplay with lean and efficient dialogue that gets the point across. The most fun aspect of the story was going through the first episode with Superfly Johnson learning that the evil corporation is chopping up people to make burgers. It was a fun few lines, short and to the point and experienced through gameplay. That's how they should have told the story.

The thing is... I can see the vision. I can definitely see the vision. A badass time-travelling romp through the ages, a legendary sword imbued with ultimate power slicing through enemies, levelling up and getting stronger to defeat the toughest baddies of all time, not by yourself but with your bros. A fast game where you're forced to use cautious tactics to ensure survival. Maybe if John Romero chose to keep his first Ion Storm game on Quake 1 engine, kept the scope in check and eventually made sequels that ramped up to the behemoth that Daikatana is, it would have turned out a lot better. However, he came out swinging fast and hard. He shot for the moon and... oops, burned up in the sun with this game.

Like I said, acquired taste. If you're an FPS freak like me you've gotta beat it at least once.
